name: Mangbetu elongated head

card.summary: The Mangbetu elongated head, or lipombo, was a Central African practice of binding infants' heads in cloth to produce an elongated skull associated with beauty and status.
card.note: Performed on infants; historical practice that began dying out in the 1950s.

quick.overview:
Among the Mangbetu people of what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, babies' heads were tightly wrapped in cloth so that the skull grew into an elongated shape. The elongated head became the group's signature look in photography and African art.

It is relevant to looks culture as a documented case of head shape being deliberately shaped for beauty and status, usually paired with elaborate hairstyles. It only works in infancy.
quick.how: Historically, cloth was bound snugly around a baby's head. This entry documents history and gives no instructions.
quick.risks: A practice carried out on infants without their consent; related head-shaping traditions are reported to cause asymmetry. It began dying out in the 1950s.

lead: Lipombo is the head elongation tradition of the Mangbetu people, in which babies' heads were bound snugly in cloth [1]. The resulting elongated head is the group's distinctive look and makes Mangbetu figures recognisable in African art [1].

Women's elaborate hairstyles, shaped to accentuate the head, were documented alongside it by photographer Casimir Zagourski in the early twentieth century [1]. In 1870 botanist Georg Schweinfurth described the Mangbetu as aristocratic and elegant, and the elongated heads stood out to European colonists [1].
The practice began dying out in the 1950s with westernisation [1].

angle.text: Shaping happened in infancy, so adults could not do it; the elongated head was a beauty and status marker and was framed by elaborate hairstyles.

paras: The Mangbetu kingdoms were integrated into the Congo Free State in 1892 [1]. The elongated heads were noted by European visitors, and Zagourski's photographs and films documented royal courts, dances and head elongation [1].
